Aesthetic Decisions:  Upon successful completion of this course, a student should be able to make individual aesthetic decisions and judgments related to their own artwork.
Critique:  Upon successful completion of this course, a student should be able to discuss, critique and evaluate their own sculptural designs, as well as those of their classmates.

Historical and Contemporary Sculpture:  Upon successful completion of this course, a student should be able to examine, compare and analyze historical and contemporary examples of sculpture through critique.

Methods and Tools:  Upon successful completion of this course, a student should be able to skillfully use a variety of methods and tools, including power tools, metal working equipment molding processes and modeling techniques at an advanced level.

Recorded Documentation:  Upon successful completion of this course, a student should be able to keep a recorded documentation in a sketchbook examining exploratory processes including aesthetics, design construction and artist references.

Sculptural Compositions:  Upon successful completion of this course, a student should be able to independently produce sculptural compositions that successfully incorporate advanced sculptural techniques.
objectives: Synthesize knowledge of contemporary sculpture.
Experiment with advanced methods of fabrication.
Design a large sculpture for a specific site.
Design and construct sculpture pieces at an advanced level.
Evaluate and discuss sculpture in critiques.
Compose an oral presentation on a contemporary sculpture and a sculpture process.

outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.

Warm-Up:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to demonstrate knowledge of the proper use of floor exercises and barre exercises with respect to the warm up of particular muscle group, and exercise for strength and flexibility.
Terminology:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to understand modern dance terminology.
Objective Analysis:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to show an appreciation for the art of modern dance, through objective analysis of a modern dance performance.
Memorize Choreography:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to memorize basic modern choreography with variance in style (option to participate in the dance concert).
Demonstrate Basic Technique:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to demonstrate basic modern dance technique (leaps, turns, jumps, and traveling steps).
Counting Music:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to count music as related to dance.
objectives: Formulate a continued progression of intermediate level warm up exercises for strength, technique, and flexibility.
Implement combinations of dance steps, jumps, turns, and leaps.
Synthesize further progression of placement and technique.
Illustrate proper utilization of the stage in large and small group formations.
Explain basic technical aspects of stage performance.
Analyze the art of modern dance through continued study and participation.
rows.objectives_lead: Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to:

rows.title: Advanced Modern Dance
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Count Music:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to show ability to count music as related to dance.

Memorize Choreography:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to memorize basic modern dance choreography with variance in style (option to participate in the dance concert).
Perform Basic Techniques:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to memorize and perform basic modern dance technique (leaps, turns, jumps, and traveling steps).
Philosophical Schools of Movement:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to identify different philosophical schools of modern dance movement.
Terminology:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to understood modern dance terminology.

Warm-Up:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to demonstrate knowledge of the proper use of floor exercises and barre exercises with respect to the warm-up of a particular muscle group, and exercises for strength and flexibility.
objectives: Implement advanced modern dance skills with emphasis on growing endurance, placement, stretch, strength, technique, muscle awareness, and transitions.
Interpret modern dance terminology and explain various philosophical schools of thought on modern dance movement.
Investigate group and individual choreography and performance opportunities.

rows.title: Intermediate Ballet

outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.

Demonstrate the Five Feet Positions and Eight Body Positions from the Classical Dance Syllabus:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to identify and demonstrate the five positions of the feet used in classical ballet, the eight body positions with correct arm and head directions that are used for a theatre (proscenium stage) presentation of classical concert dance and have the knowledge of stage directions from a performer's point of view.
The Seven Movements that Make Up Dance:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to recite and demonstrate from memory the "seven movements" of dance.
objectives: Apply knowledge of the eight positions of the body in relation to the stage and/or practice room (Cecchetti & Russian).

rows.title: Advanced Ballet, Pointe and Partnering
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Dance Review:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to critique and analyze a dance performance.  Pieces chosen are subject to approval of instructor.

Memorize Partnering Choreography:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to commit to memory and execute a minimum 128 count segment of choreography set to music chosen by the instructor that involves partnering between two dancers.  The exercise must involve the successful exchange of weight and support between the dancers.

Memorize Warm-Up Exercises:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to commit to memory a series of warm-up and strengthening exercises that are specific to working on Pointe shoes.  The student will be expected to know the appropriate order of the warm-up.

Performance:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to perform either in a classroom studio concert or in mainstage theatre presentations of the dance classes each semester they attend class.
objectives: Verify the fit of their own pointe shoes and prepare them for use in the classroom and on the stage.

Sustain positions and move through a sequence of steps while accompanied by a partner.
Execute beginning steps and positions on pointe and maintain one’s own balance in that position while being manipulated by another dancer in partnered adagio movement.

Hydrologic Cycle:  Diagram and explain the hydrologic cycle including terrestrial, atmospheric and oceanic realms and processes.
Role of Water in Weather:  Explain the role of water in weather, including its relationship to cloud formation and different forms of precipitation.
Structure of Water Molecule:  Explain the structure of the water molecule and how it is capable of absorbing and releasing energy.
Heat Budget:  Describe earth’s heat budget on planetary, seasonal, and day-night scales.
Mid-latitude Cyclone:  Describe the formation of a mid-latitude cyclone.
Wind and Pressure Belts:  Diagram Earth’s wind and pressure belts.
objectives: Explain the physical changes in state that occur with water at Earth’s surface as well as heat absorbed or emitted with each change.
Explain how heat is transferred throughout the earth system by atmospheric processes.
Explain three different ways heat is transferred at the atomic level.
Analyze various atmospheric measurements and conditions that are responsible for weather.
Describe the properties of the atmosphere and explain how they regulate Earth’s heat budget.
Diagram and explain how the atmosphere circulates.
Compare and contrast the differences between anticyclones and cyclones.
Describe the properties contained in each atmospheric layer.
Describe some of the controls on global climates.
Explain Earth-Sun relationships that are responsible for seasonality.
Explain some of the controls on global climates including natural and human-induced causes.
Illustrate general atmospheric circulation from pole to pole.
Identify disruptions to the weather/climate system including anthropogenic influences.
Describe possible ways to maintain climate conditions or reduce the pace of climate change.
Illustrate the structure of the atmosphere.
Analyze the amount of incoming solar radiation at a given latitude during the solstices and equinoxes.
Record and analyze atmospheric moisture.
Prepare and interpret a weather map.
Analyze weather data from radar, satellite and station sources.
Classify world climates and explain their distribution.
Consider data regarding El Nino and La Nina conditions and then relate that information to climate change.
Describe the transfer of energy in the atmosphere and at Earth’s surface.
Explain cloud formation at different altitudes using dew point and humidity information.
Utilize and explain different types of weather data gathering instruments.
Analyze experimental results from climate modeling using natural and anthropogenic variables, describing the influence of each on sustainable atmospheric conditions.

rows.title: Oceanography
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Global Redistribution of Heat:  Explain the role the oceans play in the global redistribution of heat as it influences climate and weather.
Diagram Energy Flow:  Diagram energy flow through a marine community and/or sustainable biomass production.
Sea Floor Topography:  Illustrate, define, and explain the origin of sea floor topography and ocean basins.

Water Molecule Origin and Influence:  Diagram and/or describe the water molecule, including chemical bonds within and between water molecules, and its properties, noting their origin and influence on oceanographic processes and qualities.
History of Ocean Exploration:  Outline highlights in the history of ocean exploration.
objectives: Lecture
Explain the origins of the ocean basins, sea floor features, and of seawater.
Explain oceanic surface and deep circulation as it relates to temperature, salinity, and gas content, noting their impact on biologic productivity.
Describe the influences of temperature and salinity on seawater density.
Describe and explain the influence the ocean has on climate and weather.
Explain the sources of marine sediments and diagram their distribution from shore to mid-ocean basin.
Describe how waves form and propagate.
Explain the causes of tides and classify different tidal forms.
Explain nutrient cycling in marine habitats.
Explain erosional and depositional processes responsible for shaping coastal land forms.
Explain the origin and use of various marine resources.
Describe the concept of sustainability as applied to the exploitation of natural resources.
Describe how resources are currently being depleted and what steps can be taken to move toward sustainable practices.
Laboratory
List the chemical composition of seawater.
Illustrate trophic levels within a marine habitat.
Classify marine organisms ecologically based on their habit and habitat.
Analyze water density of different temperatures and salinity.
Chart oceanographic surface currents given real-time sea surface temperatures.
Explain the conditions that influence productivity in a marine ecosystem.
Measure turbidity, salinity, temperature, and depth of photic zone.
Diagram Earth’s heat budget and explain the ocean's role.
Analyze sediments for biogenic and terrigenous sediments.
Conduct field trip exercises.
Apply sustainable concepts to different oceanographically produced or influenced natural resources, such as mariculture, soil (salinization), water, mineral, and ore use.

rows.title: Global Climate Change: Past, Present and Future
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Greenhouse Gases and Global Climate Conditions:  Describe the relationship between greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and global climate conditions.
Role of Oceans - Greenhouse Gases:  Relate the role of the oceans in controlling the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.
Investigative Techniques:  Explain techniques used to investigate climate conditions in earth’s past.
Climate Models:  Describe how climate models are produced and their utility in predicting future climate scenarios.
Role of Biosphere - Greenhouse Gases:  Describe the role of the biosphere, including anthrospheric influences, in controlling the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere.
Long-Term Storage of Greenhouse Gases:  Explain how long-term storage of greenhouse gases in the geosphere develops.
objectives: Explain the relationship between the sun and Earth, including orbital characteristics, solar intensity, across the latitudes, seasonality, insolation, and penetration of the solar electromagnetic spectrum through the atmosphere’s layers.
Explain the causes and results of large scale and meso-scale atmospheric circulation.
Describe the ocean's role in climate management, including heat absorption, surface current influences, and CO2 absorption.
Classify the different layers of the atmosphere.
Contrast climate and weather and understand broad controls on climate.
Explain the role of volcanism on Earth’s climate.
Identify greenhouse gases and their sources, both natural and man-made.
Explain the “Greenhouse Effect”.
Classify different components of Earth natural systems into larger groupings such as Atmosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere.
Explain the dynamics Earth’s orbit as they affect climate.
Explain Earth’s atmospheric heat budget.
Diagram the biologic pump of CO2.
Identify the sources that allow scientists to evaluate past climates.
Describe the potential for future climate change based on climate modeling and current trends.
Describe the current climate trend from as far back as 200,000 years.
Explain the role of glaciers, including the polar ice caps, on Earth and what relationships they have specifically with climate and the oceans.

rows.title: Mineralogy and Crystal Optics
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.

Origin of Optical Properties of Minerals:  Explain the origin of different optical properties of minerals such as birefringent colors as they emerge through a mineral crystal, relief, crystal shape, cement, and crystal textures.
Crystal Forms:  Recognize and classify crystal forms.
Mineral Identification:  Identify different minerals in thin sections and then correctly naming rocks base don those mineral IDs.

Physical Property Identification:  Identify a wide variety of different minerals in hand samples utilizing a wide range of physical properties and apparatuses/chemical procedures needed to correctly assess a given physical property.
Mineral Associations and Economic Use:  Know the occurrence, typical mineral associations, and economic use of a wide variety of minerals.
Descriptive Evaluations:  Produce descriptive evaluations of mineral crystal faces using Miller Indices.
objectives: Lecture
Diagram and label atomic structures given atomic number, atomic mass, and ionization state.
Explain the different types of atomic and molecular bonding and compare and contrast the chemical qualities that develop those bonds.
Model or illustrate the origin of different crystal morphologies.
Classify and describe different crystal morphologies.
Explain and define different types of physical properties minerals may possess.
Explain the relationship of the physical properties of minerals to the chemistry and crystal structure of minerals.
Define and describe the different classes of minerals.
Explain the occurrence of different minerals in relationship to different physical settings.
Explain the theory behind optical identification of minerals.
Laboratory
Identify different crystal forms.
Identify different crystal classes.
Identify and label crystal faces using Miller Indices and symmetry.
Measure crystal angles.
Explain the use of, and demonstrate the appropriate technique for, testing mineral physical properties.
Identify and classify minerals.
Explain and demonstrate the appropriate technique for identifying minerals based on optical properties.

Identify Minerals and Rocks: Identify rocks and minerals, to support explanations of rock origins.
Landforms: Recognize and explain the origin of landforms as observed in the field and in map/cybermap examples.
Basic Methods of Field Scientists: Apply the basic methods utilized by field scientists (observation, data collection, and interpretation).
Origin of northern Sierras: Recognize and explain the origin of geologic features, especially tectonostratigraphic terranes, as observed in the field and in lab samples/maps/mapping software.
objectives: Identify and classify by testing minerals and rocks relating their features to rock origins.
Analyze outcrops at field stops by assessing the materials of the site and generating interpretations as to processes that formed them.
Identify, classify, and describe geologic structures, noting the forces that are responsible for them.
Utilize topographic and geologic maps to formulate interpretations based on spatial and stratigraphic positions of features and rocks.

Based on spatial and stratigraphic positions of features and rocks, especially those locations visited on the field trip, develop a summary of gold emplacement, enrichment, exposure and placer deposition, including tectonic highlights.

Summarize climatologic and ecologic conditions as they span Alpine to foothill locations, including those visited on the field trip, while considering the northern Sierra's impact to Sacramento Valley and Basin and Range valley floor habitats.

Review the resources the northern Sierras have provided to California both currently and in the past, noting how they are the product of geologic and climatologic processes, adding in example locations and regions on a map, to be supported by sites visited on the field trip.

Identify and classify rocks and use features within them to analyze their origins as they indicate past conditions.

rows.title: California Through Time, A Geologic Journey
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
Impact of Geology:  Describe the impact geology has on California by considering the source of industrial/economic materials and geologic hazards.

Origin of Major Geologic Hazards:  Relate the origin of major geologic hazards, such as volcanism and volcano types, earthquakes and their magnitude, and tsunamis, to the specific plate tectonic settings present in California.
Major Geomorphic Provinces of California:  Identify the major geomorphic provinces of California, their locations, general geologic character, tectonic origins, and general history.
Faults and Fold Belts:  Describe faults and fold belts in California and their role in mountain-forming and morden geologic hazards.

Explain the causes of earthquake and volcanic activity in California.
Evaluate geologic hazards within different geomorphic provinces of California.
Investigate the processes that result in ore formation and emplacement.
Synthesize the occurrence of economic ores in the state with plate tectonic processes and geomorphic provinces.
Describe the various land-forming processes that dominate some of the geomorphic provinces of California.
Describe and relate California’s ground and surface water occurrences to the state’s geomorphic provinces.
Describe soil occurrences in the geomorphic provinces of California.
Describe the general geologic history of the state.

Understand the character and distribution of California's water resources, including aquifer depletion and recharge, as well as surface reservoirs, in relationship to climate, human needs, and sustainable use.
Explain and apply the principles of the scientific method.

Obtain outputs for specific inputs.
Convert equations into function form.

Given the graph or rule of a function, graph and/or express it with a horizontal and vertical shift.
Given the graph or rule of a function, graph and/or express it with a vertical/horizontal stretch or compression.
Given the graph of a function, graph and express it reflected through the x and/or y-axis.
Identify the rule (or the graph) that represents a given transformation of a function.

From the graph.
By studying a table of x/y pairs.

Parabolas with vertex at the origin of coordinates.
Ellipses centered at the origin of coordinates.
Hyperbolas with center at the origin of coordinates.
Translated parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas.

Arithmetic sequences nth term expression and partial sums.
Geometric sequences nth term expression, partial sums, and infinite series.
Solve linear, non-linear, and absolute value inequalities in one variable using algebraic methods and graphing technology.
Solve systems of:
Linear equations in two variables, using graphing and algebraic methods.
Linear inequalities in two variables using graphing methods.
Linear equations in three or more variables, using Gauss Jordan elimination and calculator technology.

objectives: Multivariable Functions
Find the limit of a function at a point.
Determine whether a function is continuous at a point.
Apply properties of limits and continuity.
Recognize the equations of commonly used surfaces (sphere, paraboloid, ellipsoid, hyperboloid, cone, plane, cylinder, etc.), and sketch these surfaces.
Sketch a surface by finding cross-sections.
Sketch a contour diagram for a function of two variables.
Sketch a level surface for a function of three variables.
Vector Operations
Find the magnitude and direction of a vector.
Use the geometric definitions of addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, dot product, and cross product to perform the vector operations.
Use the algebraic definitions of addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication, dot product, and cross product to perform the vector operations.
Project one vector onto the line in the direction of another vector.
Differentiation of Functions of Several Variables
Determine the differentiability of a function of several variables.
Use a contour diagram or a table of values for a function to estimate a partial derivative and a directional derivative.
Compute and evaluate partial derivatives algebraically.
Find the gradient vector at a point.
Compute directional derivatives.
Find a derivative using the chain rule.
Compute second-order and higher-order partial derivatives.
Applications of Differentiation
Write the equation of a tangent plane to a surface at a point.
Find the linear and quadratic approximations of a function near a point.
Use a contour diagram to find the critical points of a function and determine whether they are local maximums, local minimums, or saddle points.
Use the partial derivatives to find the critical points of a function.
Use the Second Derivative Test to determine whether a critical point is a local maximum, local minimum, or a saddle point.
Determine whether a function has a global maximum or minimum on a given domain including using limits and/or the Extreme Value Theorem when appropriate.
Use Lagrange Multipliers to find the maximum and minimum values of a function subject to a given constraint.
Integration of Functions of Several Variables
Use a contour diagram or a table of values to find a Riemann sum to approximate a double integral over a region.
Evaluate double integrals.
Use the limits of integration for a double integral to sketch the region of integration.
Reverse the order of integration on a double integral.
Evaluate triple integrals.
Use the limits of integration for a triple integral to sketch the region of integration.
Switch the order of integration on a triple integral.
Evaluate double integrals in polar coordinates.
Evaluate triple integrals in cylindrical and spherical coordinates.
Find the Jacobian.
Use a change of variables and the Jacobian to evaluate a double or triple integral.
Applications of Integration
Find the average value of a function on a region.
Use a double integral to find the area of a region.
Use a double integral to find the volume of a solid.
Use a triple integral to find the volume of a solid.
Use triple integrals to calculate the total mass and the center of mass of a solid object.
Vector-Valued Functions, Parametric Equations and Applications
Recognize parametric equations for commonly used curves (e.g., line, circle, ellipse, helix, etc.)
Use parametric equations or a vector-valued function to sketch a curve.
Use parametric equations to sketch surfaces.
Find tangent, normal, and binormal vectors.
Write parametric equations of a line through a given point and in the direction of a given vector.
Write parametric equations for a plane through a given point and containing two nonparallel vectors.
Determine whether two curves intersect.
Determine whether a curve intersects a surface.
Find the velocity and acceleration vectors.
Write parametric equations for the tangent line to a curve at a given point.
Find the length of a segment of a curve.
Vector Fields
Given a sketch of a vector field, find a possible formula for the vector field.
Given a formula for a vector field, sketch the vector field.
Draw a flow line of a vector field through a given point.
Determine whether a field is a gradient field by trying to find a potential function.
Determine whether a field is a gradient field by calculating the curl.
Calculate the divergence of a vector field.
Determine whether an indicated point is a source or a sink.
Calculate the curl of a vector field.
Line Integrals and Applications
For any field, evaluate a line integral over C by parameterizing C.
For a gradient field, evaluate a line integral over C by using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for Line Integrals.
Use Stokes’ Theorem to evaluate a line integral.
Use Green’s Theorem to evaluate a line integral over a simple closed curve C.
Use a line integral to find the work done by a force along C.
Flux Integrals and Applications
Use a surface integral with the area vector (dA) to calculate the flux of a vector field through a surface that is given by a graph of a function.
Use a surface integral with the area vector (dA) to calculate the flux of a vector field through a cylindrical surface.
Use a surface integral with the area vector (dA) to calculate the flux of a vector field through a sphere.
Use the Divergence Theorem to calculate the flux through a solid region.
Calculate the flux of a vector field through a parameterized surface.
Use a flux integral to find the area of a parameterized surface.

Methods:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to use appropriate microbiological media and analytical methods to identify a specific bacterial species.

rows.title: Mainstage Production II
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.

Upon successful completion of this class, a student should be able to notate stage blocking in a rehearsal script, to include vocal changes, line interpretation, stage blocking directions, and psychological motivations.
objectives: 1-unit objective:
Investigate, with a group of individuals, the creative process of creating staging and performing a Mainstage production.
In addition to the objective shown for the previous unit level, the 2-unit student will be able to:
Formulate in group rehearsals an understanding of stage blocking, line memorization, character development, and improvisation.
Construct scenery, paint sets, install lighting equipment, and assist with general production activities.
In addition to the objectives shown for the previous unit level, the 3-unit student will be able to:
Evaluate and analyze a script for rehearsal and performance.
Employ acting, performance and production skills as part of a Mainstage play.
Investigate the technical requirements of acting rehearsals, technical rehearsals, dress rehearsals and public performances.
Apply proficiency in auditioning for a play and undertake an acting or production role requiring moderate to intermediate performance/technical skills.
Compose characterization, stage interaction, memorization, and ensemble techniques.
In addition to the objectives shown for the previous unit level, the 4-unit student will be able to:
Create and dramatize the behavioral life of a character in rehearsal and performance.
Synthesize a production role or assignment that requires extensive character development, memorization and performance.
Integrate technical effects and backstage operations with performance.
In addition to the objectives shown for the pervious unit level, the 5-unit student will be able to:
Formulate acting and production tasks that are critical to creating the unity and stylistic elements of the small group Mainstage production.
Use and maintain production elements such as props, costumes, and furniture to create the world of a chosen production.
Implement leadership skills by completing a major performance and/or production role in a play.
In addition to the objectives shown for the previous unit level, the 6-unit student will be able to:
Recognize and demonstrate their collaborative responsibilities with the director and designers in rehearsal and in performance.
Devise skills in the design, fabrication and integration of technical elements of a production.
Demonstrate a strong work ethic within a professional framework of collaboration.

Synthesize makeup skills relative to modeling facial features, (including forehead, eyes, nose, cheeks, throat, mouth, chin and nasolabial folds) and body areas (hands, arms).

Investigate the technical requirements of acting rehearsals, technical rehearsals, dress rehearsals, and public performances.

rows.title: Repertory Theatre - Technical
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.

Terminology:  Upon successful completion of the course, a student should be able to demonstrate a working knowledge of theatrical terminology while engaging in the cooperative task(s) of developing a stage production.
objectives: The 1-unit student will be able to:
Collaborate with a group of individuals in the creative process of planning, preparing, and staging Repertory Theatre.
Implement a self-evaluation process and select an area(s) of study in consultation with instructor.
Implement Repertory Theatre work assignments on schedule and according to pre-determined guidelines.
In addition to the objectives above, the 2-unit student will be able to:

Apply skill proficiency in specific areas of Repertory Theatre:  scenery construction, fabrication and rigging; console operations; stage management; lighting; sound; costumes; wardrobe; properties; make-up; publicity; house management; concessions, and running crews.
Analyze the layout of the performing arts complex and the primary activities that are in each area.
Analyze the major technical components in the creative process of staging a repertory theatre; i.e., lighting, sound, scenery, costumes, make-up.
In addition to the objectives above, the 3-unit student will be able to:
Demonstrate proper use of power hand tools.
Complete a production project according to detailed instructions and specifications.
Compose a resume of progressive theatre work experience.

Explain Repertory Theatre production organization and identify the individual responsibilities and tasks required within a Repertory Theatre Company: first director, designers, technical director, stage manager.
In addition to the objectives above, the 4-unit student will be able to:
Serve in a major Repertory Theatre production area as a production foreman or manager.
Analyze basic lighting instruments, including fresnels, elliposicals, par-cans, strip lights, and follow spots.
Measure and cut lumber.
Solve project requirements on the basis of skills learned in laboratory sessions.
Collaborate with other students in the successful completion of a repertory theatre season.
In addition to the objectives above, the 6-unit student will be able to:
Hang, focus and color lighting instruments from the following locations, beams, electricals, coves, and stage.
Investigate set designs including floor plans, elevations, working drawings, and painters' schematics.
Apply painting techniques in creating texture, color variations, weathering, patterns, and distress.
Fulfill responsibility for a portion of a collective project, and be held accountable for the fulfillment of that commitment.
Work on "strike" crew.
Notate the blocking of actors, scenery and special effects in a rehearsal script.
Critique performance work.
Coordinate the creation of a major piece of scenery.
In addition to the objectives above, the 8-unit student will be able to:
Examine basic structural components of flats, platforms, drops, stairs, and masking elements.
Assess, research, and organize stage properties for a scripted play.
Operate the counterweight system including weighting arbors and following standard procedures.
Evaluate a light plot including instrument symbols, location, circuitry, and color media requirements.
Identify duties of the stage manager and principles and objectives of organizing rehearsals, crews, technical rehearsals, and performance procedures.
Evaluate procedures for constructing flats, platforms, and step units.
Analyze the responsibilities of a director, assistant director, designer, assistant designer, or production coordinator.

rows.title: General Zoology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Broader than Objectives, SLOs are often comprised of what the student can do as a result of combining several course objectives.
List the steps of scientific method (in proper order). Define each step. Design an experiment to test the benefits of “limbless” locomotion.
objectives: Define attributes of life and levels of biological organization.
Know ultrastructure of a typical animal cell and stages of cell cycle.
Define asexual vs sexual reproduction.
Explain various processes of development.
Compare Mendel's observations with the modern gene theory.
Compare Darwinism and a modern synthetic theory including population genetics and genetic mutation.
Explain the architecture of animals; know the variation in animal body plans.
Differentiate between taxonomy and systematics.
Describe the evolutionary history and morphology of animal-like protists.
Outline the benefits of multicellularity.
Contrast general asymmetrical body plans to radial symmetry and bilateral symmetry.
Describe the development of the coelom and dermal layers of the body.
Compare the body plans of the prominent protostome phyla Mollusca, Annelida, and Arthropoda identifying the significance of metamerism and tagmosis.
Characterize the Phylum Echinodermata and its unique radiate body plan.
Identify how animal behaviors evolve for reproductive success and reinforce reproductive isolation of species.
Identify the common features of chordates and related deuterostomes.
Compare and contrast vertebrates to primitive chordate groups identifying common traits and traits unique to vertebrates.
Explain population bottlenecks and founder effects alter alleles in a population.
Compare and contrast mechanisms for and evidence of microevolution and macroevolution.
Explain how changes in population alleles (gene pool) over time, and reproductive isolation (reduced gene flow) of populations, can lead to speciation.

Identify mechanisms that reinforce pre-mating reproductive isolation in populations, potentially leading to speciation, including: ecological (habitat), behavioral (mating cues), and temporal (timing of mating) isolation examples.
Explain how differences in mating behaviors, such as mating cues or sex pheromones,  can result in reproductive isolation between populations, ultimately leading to speciation.

Outline major events in the fossil record and geologic time-scale, including the "Cambrian Explosion" of animal Phyla, the relationship between major extinctions and taxa radiation - such as the Permian-Triassic and Cretaceous-Tertiary events.
Compare and contrast relative-dating of fossil-layers, using stratigraphy, and direct-dating of fossil-layers using radiometric dating techniques.
